text:
Admiration arrives at the worst possible time.

You get the most of it when you've done the least – the announcement, the pitch, the "I'm building this." Applause for the idea.

You get the least of it when you're doing the most – head down, six weeks in, fixing the unglamorous thing nobody sees. Silence for the work.

So if admiration is your fuel, you run out exactly when you need it most. The tank is full at the start line and empty on the climb.

Conviction is the fuel that doesn't depend on an audience being in the room.

What's powering you through the quiet part right now?

Admiration doesn't just run out. It points you the wrong way.

It's loudest for the performance of the idea – the launch post, the slick deck, the origin story – and quietest for the work that actually makes it real. The unglamorous bug fix. The tenth customer call. The pricing page rewrite.

So if you're running on admiration, you drift toward the things that get applause and away from the things that get built. You optimise for the audience, not the venture.

That's the quiet danger: not that the fuel runs dry, but that it steers.

Conviction steers by the problem instead – it asks "did this move the work forward?", not "did this get a reaction?"

Where have you caught yourself doing the thing that gets applause instead of the thing that moves the build?

You already know what you think of your idea. That's the problem.

You've lived inside it for months. Every objection, you've already answered in your head. Every risk, you've already talked yourself past. So when you go looking for feedback, you're not really looking – you're hoping.

The people close to you won't fix that. They like you. They want you to win. Their yes costs them nothing.

A second opinion is only worth something if the person giving it has nothing to gain from your yes – and isn't afraid of your no.

Who in your circle is that person?

Founder gut-check: "I love this" is not a customer.

Enthusiasm is easy to give. It costs nothing, it feels kind, and it keeps the conversation pleasant. So people hand it out freely – especially to founders they like.

Validation is different. Validation is someone changing their behaviour: paying, switching, waiting, telling a friend. That costs them something.

If you're collecting "I love this" and calling it traction, you're mistaking applause for evidence.

What's the last piece of feedback that actually cost the person something to give?

Founder gut-check: are you building a project – or a business?

A project asks "can I build this?" A business asks "will someone pay for this, again and again?"

They feel the same in the early days. Same excitement, same late nights, same demo that makes people nod.

But a project is finished when it works. A business is only starting when it works – because now it has to be found, sold, supported, and paid for by strangers who don't care how clever it is.

Most things that die weren't bad projects. They were projects that never became businesses.

Which one are you actually building right now?

Most founders go looking for the yes. The dangerous ones go looking for the no.

A yes feels good and tells you almost nothing – people say yes to be nice, to be encouraging, to end the conversation.

A no, if you can find an honest one, tells you exactly where the idea is weak while it's still cheap to fix.

So the most useful question isn't "what do you like about this?" It's "what would stop you from paying for this?" – and then sitting quietly while they answer.

When did you last go hunting for the no instead of the yes?

Founder-market fit isn't one thing. It's two, and people confuse them constantly.

The first: do you understand this market better than almost anyone? Lived it, worked in it, felt the problem in your own hands.

The second: will you still be here in three years, when it's boring and hard and no one's clapping?

Insight without endurance fades. Endurance without insight builds the wrong thing beautifully.

You need both. Which one is your strong side – and which are you quietly hoping won't matter?

Ask yourself what result would make you stop.

Not slow down. Stop.

If there's no number, no answer, no single piece of evidence that would actually kill the idea for you, you're not evaluating it. You're building a case for a verdict you already reached.

Founders spend four months validating an idea they were always going to build regardless of what the validation said. That research wasn't a decision-making tool. It was a delay with better PR.

So: what would make you stop?

text:
The build-or-don't decision needs three things. Most founders skip straight past all of them.

Who pays – a person you could put a name to, not "the market".

What they'd stop doing, or stop paying for, to pay you instead.

The number that makes you walk away, decided before you're three months and a chunk of your savings into finding out.

Skip any of the three and you haven't made the decision. You've deferred it to a future version of yourself who'll have a lot more sunk into being right.

Which of the three can you answer right now, without hedging?

text:
"Just ship something small and let the market tell you."

Fair – for working out the shape of the product. It's the wrong tool for deciding whether to build at all.

"What should we build" and "should we build" aren't the same question, and the second is the one people dodge by rushing to the first.

Building something small still costs you months. It isn't free just because it's fast. And if you'd have built it regardless of what it told you, the market didn't decide anything. You did, before you started, and the build was theatre.

What would the small thing have to show you before you'd actually stop?
